title: Network egress confinement
subtitle: The most privileged agent seat in my estate is fenced: its only way out is a proxy that allows a handful of exact destinations.
lede: AgentOS runs coding agents in containers, and the team-lead seat is the most privileged of them. It directs other agents and uses the estate's governance tools. My view was that a seat like that should reach its model vendor and nothing else, so I built deny-by-default network confinement for it. The seat's container sits on an internal network with no route out. Its one exit is an allow-listing proxy, and the proxy carries one thing: an encrypted connection to the seat's vendor endpoints. An allow-list has well-known ways around it, and each is closed explicitly. The seat cannot reconfigure the proxy, and when the proxy is full it refuses new tunnels.
quote: I treat the agent's network as an attack surface and start from deny-all with one named exit.
evidence: Zero-trust and egress control: deny-by-default network confinement for the most privileged agent seat, whose one exit is an allow-listing proxy to its vendor endpoints.
Allow-list bypass prevention: names resolving into private address space, mismatched TLS host names, wildcards and address literals all refused.
Proof-driven rollout: every rollout probes that the vendor path succeeds and every blocked category fails, and a preflight checks the proxy image identity before a seat starts.
author: Corey James
